lore_summary.en: Ferdowsi's Alexander carries both philosophy and a sword. He is Iranian by a twist of blood — and the world bows.
lore_summary.fa: اسکندر ذوالقرنین با شکست دادن دارا بر ایران دست یافت، اما آشکار شد که نیمه‌برادر او بوده. او جهان را فتح کرد، در جستجوی آب حیات بود و به سرزمین‌های دور رفت. وقتی جوان درگذشت، خواست دستانش از کفن بیرون باشد — تا نشان دهد که از جهان هیچ نبرده است.

scenes.body_en: Sekandar arrived in Iran not merely as a conqueror but as something stranger — a man who claimed to belong to the country he was taking apart. The Shahnameh carries a tradition that his mother was the daughter of Darab, sent away in secret because her breath smelled of herbs and the king found her disagreeable. Philip of Macedon had taken her in, married her, and Sekandar was born. This made him the half-brother of Dara, the man he had just defeated in battle. He had not known it until Dara lay dying.

That knowledge changed the shape of everything. Sekandar wept over Dara's body and swore vengeance on the two ministers who had stabbed their own king to end the war quickly. He executed them. He took Dara's daughter Roshanak as his wife, absorbing the Achaemenid line rather than erasing it. The chronicle does not let him be a pure destroyer. He arrives carrying Iranian blood, and he acts on it.

What followed was a life of movement — east and east and east again, through the known world and past its edges. Sekandar did not rest the way other kings rested. He met philosophers and debated them. He descended into the sea in a glass vessel to observe what lived in the deep. He sought the Well of Immortality in the Land of Darkness, sending his cook ahead to prepare food — and it was the cook, not Sekandar, who accidentally drank from the spring when a dried fish came back to life in his hands. The king came close to living forever but did not reach it.

He is called Two-Horned — Dhul-Qarnayn — though the Shahnameh does not settle on why. Some say it was because he ruled both East and West. Some say it was a helmet. Some say it was a mark of the divine. The ambiguity is kept. Ferdowsi was not interested in resolving it.

When Sekandar died, he was young enough that it seemed like an error. He asked that he be carried to his tomb with his hands outside the shroud, open and empty. He had conquered the world. He was taking nothing out of it. The philosophers who followed him were supposed to speak at his burial and explain what his life had meant. One by one, they refused. None of them had anything to say that would not sound hollow next to the open hands.

Ferdowsi was writing under a sultan who himself ruled through conquest — Mahmud of Ghazni, a Turkic warlord who had claimed the eastern Iranian world through military force. The Sekandar episode was therefore not a distant myth. It was a mirror. Ferdowsi gave the Greek conqueror Iranian blood and Iranian grief to carry, making the question of legitimacy through lineage versus legitimacy through power something every reader at the Ghaznavid court would feel without being told to.

The problem of writing about someone history remembers as a destroyer who believed himself a civilizer. Ferdowsi's solution was genealogical — make Sekandar partly Iranian, let him weep over Dara's body, and then let him ask questions that no conqueror had thought to ask before. The chronicle does not forgive him for the destruction, but it refuses to dismiss him either.

Sekandar is the last king in the chronicle who came from outside the Iranian tradition and was absorbed into it. After him, the kings are purely Sasanian — internal struggles, not foreign absorption. His story establishes that the Shahnameh's world can survive invasion if it can convert the invader into someone who weeps over what he has destroyed. The open hands at his burial became one of the Shahnameh's most lasting images: the conqueror who owned the world and held none of it.
scenes.body_fa: فردوسی زیر سلطه سلطانی می‌نوشت که خود از راه فتح به قدرت رسیده بود — محمود غزنوی، جنگاوری ترک که دنیای شرقی ایران را با زور تصرف کرده بود. داستان اسکندر بنابراین داستانی دور نبود — آینه‌ای بود. فردوسی به فاتح یونانی خون ایرانی و غم ایرانی داد تا پرسش مشروعیت از طریق تبار در برابر مشروعیت از طریق قدرت را بدون گفتن صریح به هر خواننده‌ای در دربار غزنوی احساس کند.
